transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-22
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 45 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Marta Diaz (Redwood CSM), Jordan Lee (NimbleHealth CTO), Samir Patel (NimbleHealth ML Eng), Elena Gomez (NimbleHealth Infra), Rita Chen (NimbleHealth PM)

Summary: quick review of this week's benchmark run comparing Redwood dedicated config vs their baseline provider. Focus on latency P95/P99, throughput (tokens/sec), and tuning knobs (batch size, quantization, KV cache).

Transcript:
[00:00] Alex Rivera: hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll keep this to about 45 minutes. quick roll call?
[00:03] Jordan Lee: jordan here.
[00:04] Samir Patel: samir.
[00:05] Elena Gomez: elena.
[00:06] Rita Chen: rita.
[00:07] Priya Shah: priya from redwood.
[00:08] Marta Diaz: marta here.
[00:10] Alex Rivera: awesome okay, agenda - go over the bench results we dropped in the doc, talk tuning suggestions and security asks, then agree on next steps. Priya you wanna kick off with the numbers?
[00:15] Priya Shah: sure, i'll share my screen, so the run we did this week was a mixed profile: 70% short prompts (<=256 tokens), 20% medium (512-2k), and 10% long (4k-8k). baseline provider numbers are the ones nimble shared last week, we tried to mirror their workload. high-level - for short prompts baseline is slightly faster at P50 by ~10ms, but for medium+long our dedicated config shows better P95 and throughput. P95 for 2k requests improved from 420ms baseline to ~310ms on redwood with batching and optimized kernels.
[00:45] Samir Patel: can you repeat that, 310ms p95 for 2k? that seems optimistic, what's the hardware and model?
[00:50] Priya Shah: yes, we used the open-llama-70b-quant variant pinned in the POC environment, running on A100-ish equivalent instances in dedicated pool, with int8 quant and kernel selection tuned, plus active KV caching for repeated prefixes. baseline was running the same model on their managed endpoints but with stock configs, no kv cache.
[01:10] Jordan Lee: curious about the accuracy impact - any hallucination or token differences with the quant profiles?
[01:15] Priya Shah: good question - we ran the eval harness against the customer prompt set, quality delta was negligible for int8 on most prompts, we have a couple of edge cases where scoring dropped ~1-2% on longer context, we flagged those in the notes.
[01:30] Rita Chen: are those edge cases from our medical prompts? if so we need to be careful.
[01:34] Priya Shah: yes some are medically dense prompts; we'll list them separately so engineering can triage.
[01:40] Alex Rivera: a quick note on throughput - for long sequences the continuous batching and kv cache reduced redundant compute, so tokens/sec improved by ~22% vs baseline for the 8k flows. For short prompts the baseline's autoscaling latency optimization gave them slightly better P50.
[01:59] Elena Gomez: those numbers are helpful. what about P99 tail? that's what worries our ops.
[02:03] Priya Shah: p99 was 1.2s baseline vs 0.95s redwood for the long workloads; for shorts baseline had p99 ~ 0.35s vs our 0.38s, so roughly on-par. The tail improvements come from our fallback routing and capacity isolation so noisy neighbors are less of an issue in dedicated.
[02:30] Samir Patel: can you explain the fallback routing bit? sometimes the baseline provider just spikes.
[02:35] Priya Shah: sure, so policy-based routing: requests can be routed to a lower-cost model variant or to a different capacity pool when latencies spike; we also keep model pinning so you choose which variants are allowed. In practice for the POC we had an auto-fallback to a 70b-quant variant that maintains semantics but reduces kernel overhead during cluster pressure.
[02:56] Jordan Lee: okay, on the cost side - your docs show lower cost per token for long sequences but higher for short ones. can you walk pricing scenarios?
[03:03] Alex Rivera: yes basically cost crossover point is around ~350 tokens. below that, the baseline's per-request optimizations beat us; above that our batching and caching saves tokens and compute. i'll send a modelled spreadsheet with different mixes, but rough numbers: for 1M short queries (~150 tokens) baseline estimated $X, our estimated slightly higher; for 100k long queries (3k tokens) we come in ~25% cheaper. we'll email the exact sheet.
[03:30] Rita Chen: pls include a break-even analysis for our mix - that's critical for finance.
[03:33] Alex Rivera: noted.
[03:35] Priya Shah: quick note on tuning knobs we recommend: 1) enable KV/prefix cache for repeated conversational flows, 2) use moderate batch sizes for medium requests (batch size 8-16 depending on latency SLO), 3) apply int8 quant but run targeted eval on medical prompts. Those three moved the needle the most in our runs.
[04:00] Samir Patel: about batching - does that increase latency for single-user interactive sessions? we worry about UX.
[04:05] Priya Shah: there's a tradeoff - we do dynamic batching with latency targets, so interactive sessions won't wait for large batches; batching is more effective for bursty APIs. We can tune to keep P95 under your SLO (you mentioned 500ms).
[04:20] Jordan Lee: we did mention 500ms P95 yes. given these numbers, seems promising for our longer analytics flows. but security - we need to run this in our VPC and ensure KMS integration. what's the plan?
[04:33] Marta Diaz: we have a private deployment option; for POC we can spin up a private control plane that talks over your VPC peering and integrate with your KMS/HSM. we'll share our SOC2 artifact and the security packet.
[04:45] Elena Gomez: do you support SSO and fine-grained RBAC for model access? we need audit logs for each request.
[04:50] Marta Diaz: yes SAML/SSO, RBAC, and per-request audit logging are supported. I'll attach the packet and a sample audit export.
[04:58] Rita Chen: timeline on SOC2 docs?
[05:00] Marta Diaz: i'll upload them by monday (we said due 2026-04-26 in action items).
[05:05] Samir Patel: there were a couple of weird transcriptions around "KV cash" in the doc - please confirm it's KV cache. small typo but confused engineers reading the sheet.
[05:12] Priya Shah: yes that's a transcription artifact, it's KV cache. we'll update the notes.
[05:18] Alex Rivera: also noted a few numbers in the run where our sampling of the baseline trace didn't have the same concurrency pattern - Priya, can we call out the concurrency differences?
[05:25] Priya Shah: sure. baseline traces had shorter but more frequent spikes; our synthetic runner had slightly higher sustained concurrency which benefits batching. we'll annotate the runs and upload raw traces so they can be re-run with exact concurrency.
[05:40] Jordan Lee: for the 24h run we will mirror production concurrency - Samir will take this on.
[05:45] Samir Patel: yep i'll run the 24h overnight and share traces + flamegraphs.
[05:50] Alex Rivera: perfect. any blockers on your side for the next steps?
[05:53] Jordan Lee: security review is the main one, plus finance needs the cost model. once we have those and the 24h run, we can decide whether to move to a dedicated pilot.
[06:05] Alex Rivera: great, recap of next steps: i send pricing & infra diagram 4/23, priya uploads logs 4/24, marta sends SOC2 package 4/26, samir runs 24h and shares results 4/30. schedule the security deep-dive for week of 4/27.
[06:20] Rita Chen: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[06:22] Priya Shah: thanks all - we'll follow up in email with the artifacts.
[06:25] Alex Rivera: thanks, meeting adjourned.

Notes: transcription contains minor mis-hearings (eg. "KV cash" -> "KV cache"). Links shared in chat: "benchmark_grafana_link" (internal), "poc_cost_model_v2.xlsx".

End of transcript.
